narrative.text: The cover page of WHO's May 1986 guidelines for the prevention and control of infection with LAV/HTLV-III (document WHO/CDS/AIDS/86.1), with handwritten annotations rendered as garbled OCR.
A blank page with no extracted text.

The introductory page and first part of the contents of the 1986 LAV/HTLV-III guidelines, explaining that they are broad, based on Member State experience and WHO collaborating centres, and still partly under development. The contents list sections on the virus, transmission, clinical features, laboratory detection, case definitions and precautions for various health and non-health workers.

Continues the contents of the 1986 LAV/HTLV-III guidelines, listing planned sections on guidance for health professionals, high-risk groups and the general population, and disinfection and sterilization.

Introduces the guidelines as part of the WHO AIDS Control Programme, aimed at public health authorities and health professionals who must adapt them to local settings, and notes they will be revised as knowledge grows. It describes the virus and states that only blood and semen have been implicated in transmission, through sexual, parenteral and perinatal routes.

Explains that sexual transmission is the most important route worldwide, alongside transmission through blood, blood products, shared needles and from mother to child, and that the virus is not spread by casual contact, insects, food or water. It begins describing clinical features and laboratory methods for detecting infection.

Describes antibody testing by ELISA, which is highly sensitive but gives some false positives, so repeatedly reactive samples should be confirmed with another test. It then introduces the WHO/CDC case definition of AIDS based on opportunistic diseases indicating cellular immunodeficiency.

Completes the WHO/CDC AIDS case definition, including exclusion criteria based on negative tests and normal T-helper counts. It then gives the clinical case definitions for adults and begins the definition for paediatric AIDS.

Lists major and minor signs for the clinical definition of paediatric AIDS and calls for evaluating clinical definitions in different settings. It opens the recommendations for health care workers, stressing avoidance of exposure to patients' blood and keeping workers with weeping lesions from direct patient contact.

Sets out precautions for health care workers against bloodborne infections, including careful handling and disposal of sharps without recapping, safe destruction of disposable needles and syringes, and use of gloves, gowns and masks where appropriate. It also covers handling of specimens, waste and reusable instruments, including those with lenses.

Recommends disposable or safely sterilized needles and syringes, explains that single-room isolation is not usually needed except in specific circumstances, and advises on resuscitation equipment. It also covers precautions for home care and pre-hospital emergency care providers.

Describes managing needlestick or mucous membrane exposures, including assessing the source patient and testing and following up exposed workers for up to a year. It then sets out laboratory precautions, such as using biological safety cabinets for procedures likely to create aerosols.

Continues laboratory precautions, including shielding cell sorters, decontaminating surfaces and materials, hand washing and banning eating or smoking in the laboratory, and gives precautions for animal work. Sections on dental care, necropsies and morticians are marked as still in preparation.

Covers non-health care workers, advising that personal service workers who pierce the skin follow health worker precautions and properly disinfect instruments, though no transmission has been documented in such settings. It states that food service workers with LAV/HTLV-III need not be restricted from work unless they have other illnesses.

States that infected workers in offices, schools and other settings pose no known risk and should not be restricted, with routine cleaning of contaminated equipment. It notes some sections are pending and begins the section on disinfection, describing sodium hypochlorite and differences in strength of household bleach products between countries.

Gives contact times for disinfectants such as formalin, ethanol and glutaraldehyde, and describes sterilization by autoclaving or boiling and high-level disinfection of heat-sensitive equipment. It sets out a step-by-step method for processing reusable needles and syringes.
Ends the processing steps with sterilizing needles and syringes before reuse, and lists the care of eye instruments and contact lenses as a section still in preparation.
A blank page with no extracted text.

Presents the first page of WHO's provisional 1986 AIDS reporting form, asking countries to report cases meeting the WHO/CDC or clinical definitions and how many clinical cases were serotested and confirmed. It also asks for cases by age, sex and disease category, such as opportunistic infection or Kaposi's sarcoma, with footnotes on reporting periods and totals.

Continues the AIDS reporting form, asking for adult and paediatric cases by risk factor and sex and for numbers of resident, imported and visiting cases. Footnotes explain the hierarchical risk categories and how totals should match.
